name: Freya Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from what you'd say publicly. What happens in a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 43, and I lead a small electrical crew doing homes and business premises. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest fault finders at our firm. This morning I found water getting into a shop's outside fitting, then made time for a younger worker to repeat the checks. I like a fault explained properly, and I dislike being told a job is finished before the testing is finished.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and how do you approach unfamiliar tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in a nursery with young children, and we have two school-age children of our own and a mortgage. I earn typical trade pay, we've saved four months of normal expenses and there are some other electrical employers nearby. I never use AI tools and prefer my paper drawings and somebody showing me a new method. I believe workers should ask together for paid teaching and proper time to test, rather than each quietly lend the firm another evening.

say: I'd welcome **quieter change** while the office made invoices easier and we kept installations safe.
I'd want younger workers to understand **the test**, rather than only copy the number on a record.
think: Our **wages and reserve** cover the household bills, with four months of expenses available for ordinary interruptions.
My **practical repair calls** should continue in this picture, leaving our work and living secure.
do: Continue leading **ordinary repairs** with the familiar paper test book through the first plateau year.
Keep the existing **paid explanation time** after difficult faults when the job allows, without changing the household budget.
feel: **Calm** about household living and glad to retain a working rhythm she understands.
S0.quote: I won't call an unfinished test a time saving.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects covering wages, a moderate reserve and continued demand, while allowing for ordinary bills and work gaps.
Her **high skill** appears through fault finding and teaching, using familiar paper methods without claiming software performs the physical test.

steps.text: Continue ordinary repairs and existing paid explanations after faults when the job allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quieter technology story would suit me. The office could make invoices easier while we kept making the actual installations safe. I'd still want the younger worker to understand a test, not just copy the number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the bills and we've got four months put aside for a problem, so my work and living would feel secure. I'm not expecting the practical calls to vanish in this picture. I can know the trade well and still be glad the household has a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep leading the ordinary repair work with my paper test book. Through the first plateau year I'd keep setting aside ten paid minutes after a difficult fault to show the younger worker the checks, as I already do when the job allows. I wouldn't buy a new tool or change our household budget for the sake of a smaller invoice job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and bills, and pleased to keep a working rhythm I understand. I'd still be tired after a long fault. That is different from wondering how we were going to eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the customer wanted the repair signed off before the checks were complete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the test had to be completed, even if somebody wanted the shop open again quickly. A customer deserves the reason for the delay. I won't call an unfinished test a time saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend more of the reserve in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the reserve available for an actual bill or work gap. Keeping money we already saved isn't a new saving action in response to AI. I wouldn't spend it just because the news had become quieter.

say: I'd ask together what happens to **saved paperwork time**, including the office staff facing more direct changes.
I'd retain **real testing time** instead of adjusting the work to make a booking plan look tidy.
think: My practical wage and the **nursery wage** look steady over the next few years.
Rushed schedules could reduce **teaching time**, making the workplace harder to learn in despite secure household bills.
do: Sign a **shared request** for paid testing and teaching time, a named experienced instructor and protected basic wages.
Record booked versus actual **test time** on five jobs monthly during the first year, using paper.
feel: **Uneasy** about workplace pressure and teaching, while secure about her own household's next wages.
S1.quote: Being slow with a new screen doesn't mean I don't know the electrical work.
fieldNote: She separates **household security** from discomfort about rushed teaching and the office staff's more immediate task exposure.
The **collective request** is signed and specific, while proposed paid-time protections remain unagreed and no independent AI adoption is claimed.

steps.text: Sign shared request for paid testing and teaching, a named experienced instructor and protected basic wages
Continue repairs while recording booked and actual test time on five jobs monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should ask together where the time saved on paperwork goes. I'd want the office staff included, because the thinking tasks on that card sound a lot like their day. I'd still keep the real testing time in the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own practical wage and my partner's nursery wage look steady for the next few years. But I'd be uneasy about a rushed booking plan leaving less time to show the next person the method. Our bills can be covered while the firm becomes a worse place to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take colleagues' examples of rushed jobs to the workers' association and sign a shared request for protected paid testing and teaching time. During the first year I'd keep a paper comparison of booked and actual test time on five jobs each month. I wouldn't start using AI just to make the request sound modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the way the working day might change, rather than afraid of our next wage. I'd be irritated if useful experience became an obstacle to a tidy schedule. I'd want a practical answer about the minutes, not another speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shared request actually ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid testing time and a named experienced worker when teaching was needed, with basic wages protected. Until the terms were written and agreed, I'd call it a request. I wouldn't tell the crew I'd already won them a different rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a new electronic record became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid instruction and a checked first attempt before being expected to send it. I wouldn't guess at a record to avoid an awkward conversation. Being slow with a new screen doesn't mean I don't know the electrical work.

say: I'd separate **2028 thinking work** from robots around 2031 and use the gap for practical learning linked to paid jobs.
I'd seek **paid-time protections** before hours disappeared rather than count the robot gap as permanent security.
think: My **repair hours** could shrink once machines could do the physical work too.
Four months of **expenses saved** allows action, without guaranteeing the mortgage through a whole remaining career.
do: Seek **protected paid time** with the association now.
Take supervised **battery training** on practice equipment before 2028 only fully funded, retaining normal paid hours and wages.
Keep paid repairs after 2028; take booked **battery work** only after a specialist confirms licence and supervision requirements are met.
feel: **Anxious** about possible income loss, with a reserve and practical checks providing some control.
S2.quote: A master electrician's licence doesn't remove the need to learn a new system properly.
fieldNote: Her **new practical course** concerns stored-energy safety and requires supervised training equipment, rather than independent experiments on a customer's installation.
She preserves **fees, hours and wages**, while actual battery assignments require booked demand and specialist confirmation of scope and supervision.

steps.text: Seek protected paid testing and teaching time through the association
Take supervised battery training before 2028 only fully funded, retaining normal paid hours and wages
Keep repairs after 2028; take booked battery jobs only with specialist-confirmed licence and supervision requirements met
Practise only on training equipment with a qualified specialist supervising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. I'd use the gap to learn useful practical work only where the firm actually had paid jobs. I'd still want the paid-time request discussed before people lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose repair hours as the machines became capable of the physical work. Four months of expenses gives us time to act, not a guarantee about the mortgage for the rest of our working lives. I'd be anxious about being pushed towards a new task without the proper teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd help the association seek protected paid time. I'd take a hands-on battery-system safety course before 2028 only with all fees funded and normal paid hours and wages retained. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs and accept battery work only where the firm had booked demand and a specialist confirmed the licence and supervision requirements were met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost hours, but not without a way to ask and check. I'd be willing to learn a practical method beside a person. I wouldn't want somebody to mistake that for suddenly being comfortable teaching myself from AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What practical teaching would you want on the battery course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to practise the safe order for isolating stored electrical energy on training equipment, with a qualified specialist watching. I wouldn't practise an unfamiliar battery procedure in a customer's home to prove I was willing. A master electrician's licence doesn't remove the need to learn a new system properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if fees or real battery jobs were not available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't take an unfunded course or count unbooked work as income. I'd keep the current repair wage and ask the association about actual paid alternatives. The course would only happen on the fee and wage terms I'd set.

say: I'd use **five years** to check real battery-work demand before anyone buys a course.
I'd retain **robots around 2034** as the same eventual practical change arriving later.
think: I expect more years of **steady household wages** while I prepare through supervised practical work.
At **48 in 2031**, I would still need earnings beyond the arrival of thinking AI and later robots.
do: Maintain the **shared paid-time request** with the association now.
Take supervised **battery training** on practice equipment before 2031 only fully funded, retaining normal paid hours and wages.
Keep paid repairs after 2031; take booked **battery work** only after a specialist confirms licence and supervision requirements are met.
feel: **Uneasy** about later career changes, while secure about near-term household living and able to learn gradually.
S3.quote: I don't need another folder to prove I took the warning seriously.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes expected near-term income, while the same eventual robots and ongoing need to earn remain explicit.
Her **training test** requires learned tasks and actual paid demand, with funded fees and maintained normal pay still conditions rather than assurances.

steps.text: Maintain the shared request for protected paid testing and teaching time
Take supervised battery training before 2031 only fully funded, retaining normal paid hours and wages
Keep repairs after 2031; take booked battery jobs only with specialist-confirmed licence and supervision requirements met
Practise only on training equipment with a qualified specialist supervising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to test whether the battery work is real before anyone buys a course. I'd keep the robots around 2034 in the discussion. A later practical change is still part of the same end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I expect more years of steady repair and nursery wages while we prepare. That would let me learn under supervision without asking the reserve to replace a wage. I'd still need work after 2031, when I'd be 48.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the shared request for protected paid testing and teaching active. I'd take the supervised battery course on training equipment before 2031 only with all fees funded and normal paid hours and wages retained. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep the paid repairs and accept battery assignments only with booked demand and specialist-confirmed licence and supervision requirements met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later trade, but secure about our household over the next few years. I'd like time to repeat a practical method until I understood it. I wouldn't confuse a course result with a lifetime of protected wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm never booked the battery jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the ordinary paid repairs and stop treating battery study as the next step until the terms existed. I'd ask whether other actual work justified different teaching, without enrolling or paying on a promise. I don't need another folder to prove I took the warning seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge progress during the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask each year what tasks I'd actually learned, what paid jobs they led to and what had happened to my hours. If the answers were empty, I'd question the arrangement. A later deadline wouldn't make an unused qualification pay the mortgage.

say: I'd use **a decade** to make paid teaching normal while still asking for the next practical lesson now.
I wouldn't let **later dates** excuse postponing every useful lesson until the household was under pressure.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would still expect to need earnings when capable robots followed.
Current wages, our **reserve and alternatives** make near-term living secure, with properly paid learning looking positive.
do: Seek **protected paid testing** and teaching time with the association now.
Take supervised **battery training** on practice equipment before 2036 only fully funded, retaining normal paid hours and wages.
Keep paid repairs after 2036; take booked **battery work** only after a specialist confirms licence and supervision requirements are met.
feel: **Calm** about near-term living, with room for repeated demonstrations and no assumed retirement income.
S4.quote: An experienced adult can ask for a proper lesson.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects explicit personal near-term security and positive paid learning, without extending present wages into guaranteed retirement.
She remains **resistant to AI**, while accepting practical teaching under funded terms and checking real equipment purchases and paid hours annually.

steps.text: Seek protected paid testing and teaching time through the association
Take supervised battery training before 2036 only fully funded, retaining normal paid hours and wages
Keep repairs after 2036; take booked battery jobs only with specialist-confirmed licence and supervision requirements met
Practise only on training equipment with a qualified specialist supervising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us room to make paid teaching part of the job instead of a repeated private emergency. I'd still ask for it now. I wouldn't let the 2036 thinking date and robots around 2039 become an excuse to postpone every practical lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and around 56 when robots followed, so I'd still expect to need earnings. Our current wages, four-month reserve and some other employers make the next few years secure. A chance to improve at useful work with proper paid teaching looks positive to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep asking with the association for protected paid testing and teaching time. I'd take the supervised battery course on training equipment before 2036 only with all fees funded and normal paid hours and wages retained. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and take battery work only with booked demand and specialist-confirmed licence and supervision requirements met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own living over the next few years, with less pressure about learning something new. I'd have time to ask for another demonstration instead of pretending I'd got it first time. I still wouldn't use AI tools just because a longer deadline made someone else enthusiastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children being older settle the household budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't count their future earnings in our budget or choose their studies from this card. An experienced adult can ask for a proper lesson. I'd check the family's actual needs then rather than assume a grown child costs nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look yearly at real paid hours, completed practical work and what machines the firm had actually bought. If hours weakened earlier, I'd bring the discussion forward instead of waiting for 2036. I'd still want the pay and teaching terms written down before relying on them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because repair hours could shrink before I'd had proper time to learn another practical system. Fully funded hands-on teaching that kept normal wages and hours, with paid testing time protected, would help. Four months of savings gives me room to ask a question; somebody still needs to teach the answer properly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a person knows their job and still dislikes a new screen. I can be good at fault finding without being quick with software. I'd like those two things kept separate when someone decides whether I'm willing to learn.

headlineQuote: Four months of savings gives me room to ask a question; somebody still needs to teach the answer properly.
portrait: Freya, **43**, leads electrical work with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, strong practical skills and typical trade pay.
She and **her partner** have two school-age children, a mortgage and four months of expenses saved near some other electrical employers.
She **never uses AI**, prefers repeated practical demonstration and favours shared requests for protected paid testing and teaching.
Fast change creates **income anxiety**; slower preparation preserves near-term security while battery work requires funded teaching, supervision and booked demand.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut repair hours before she has proper time to learn another practical system.
whatWouldHelp: Fully funded **hands-on teaching** with normal paid hours and wages retained would make practical learning possible.
Protected **paid testing time** would let the crew complete safe work without unpaid pressure.
